articles.title: In Vitro and In Vivo Effects ofExtracts on Osteoclast Differentiation
articles.full_text:
1. Introduction

Bone is continuously being resorbed by osteoclasts and formed by osteoblasts [,]. Balancing the activities of osteoclasts and osteoblasts is important in the bone remodeling process. An impaired balance leads to bone diseases such as osteoporosis, Paget’s disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and periodontal disease due to excessive activity and/or an increased number of osteoclasts []. Therefore, controlling the activity and number of osteoclasts is important in patients with bone disease.

Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells of myeloid lineage origin that can degrade the bone matrix and decalcify via proteolytic degradation and decalcification, respectively []. They are tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase-positive multinucleated osteoclast cells (TRAP-MNCs) differentiated from macrophages by macrophage colony-stimulating factor 1 (M-CSF) and receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL), which are expressed by osteoblasts [].

RANKL, an osteoclast differentiation factor, is a type II membrane protein and a member of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily []. The binding of RANKL to its receptor, RANK, on osteoclast precursors trigger the osteoclast differentiation []. The RANKL/RANK system directly regulates osteoclastogenesis and bone remodeling. RANKL/RANK signaling ultimately induces nuclear factor of activated T-cells, cytoplasmic 1 (NFATc1), a key factor in osteoclastogenesis []. NFATc1 regulates osteoclast differentiation-related genes, such as TRAP, cathepsin K, and dendritic cell-specific transmembrane protein (DC-STAMP) [,,].

Seaweeds are sources of products that are useful in many fields including food technology, biotechnology, and even medicine [,].is a species of red algae that is used as a food in Japan and Korea and is known to be effective in osteoporosis. In this study, we investigated the effects of the acid extracts of(GE) on osteoclastogenesis that play a vital role in osteoporosis.

2. Experimental Section

2.1. Extract of

An entire plant of(Inseong, Jangheung, Korea) was washed under running tap water to remove salt after drying at room temperature. The sample was washed and dried until the salt was completely drained. Three liters of water was added to 200 g of the dried sample and allowed to stand for one day. Then, 15 g of citric acid anhydrous and 150 mL of glacial acetic acid was added to the sample, which was then allowed to stand at room temperature for 4 h. The extract supernatant was filtered using Whatman No. 2 filter paper (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) before being transferred into pre-weighed containers, and the sample was concentrated with a rotary evaporator and freeze-dried to produce crude extracts.

2.2. Cell Cultures and Osteoclast Differentiation

This study was carried out in strict accordance with the recommendations contained in the Standard Protocol for Animal Study of Sunchon National University (SCNU, Suncheon, Korea). The protocol was approved by the Sunchon National University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) with Permit No. SCNU IACUC 2016-07. All efforts were made to minimize suffering.

To obtain bone marrow macrophages (BMMs), bone marrow cells (BMCs) were isolated from the femur and tibia of two mice of 5-week-old male imprinting control region (ICR) strain (Damool Science, Daejeon, Korea) by flushing with α-minimum essential medium (α-MEM; Invitrogen Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, USA) supplemented with antibiotics (100 units/mL penicillin and 100 µg/mL streptomycin; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). BMMs were obtained from BMCs cultured on a petri dish in α-MEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Invitrogen Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA, USA) with 30 ng/mL mouse recombinant macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF; PEPROTECH, Rocky HilI, NJ, USA) for 3 days. BMMs were seeded and cultured in the presence of 10 ng/mL mouse recombinant RANKL (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA) and 30 ng/mL M-CSF for 4 days in the presence or absence of extracts.

2.3. Cytotoxicity Assay for Extract of

BMMs were plated in a 96-well plate in triplicate at a density of 10,000 cells/well, and the cells were treated with 30 ng/mL M-CSF and GE. After culturing for 3 days, cell viability was evaluated with a CCK-8 kit (Dojindo Molecular Technologies, Kumamoto, Japan) according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

2.4. Tartrate-Resistant Acid Phosphatase Staining Assay

Cultured cells were fixed with 3.7% formalin for 5 min, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 10 min, and stained with TRAP solution (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) for 10 min. TRAP-multinucleated cells (cells with 3 nuclei or more; 3 ≤) were deemed as mature osteoclasts.

2.5. Western Blot Analysis

Western blotting was performed as described previously []. Cells were washed with phosphate-buffer saline (PBS) and lysed in a lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100, 1 mM sodium fluoride, 1 mM sodium vanadate, and 1% deoxycholate) supplemented with 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF; Bio Basic, Markham, CA, USA) and 5 μg/mL leupeptin (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The cell lysates were separated by centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 12 min. The proteins (20 μg) were subjected to 10% sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and then transferred onto a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane (Amersham Biosciences, Piscataway, NJ, USA). The membrane was blocked with 5% skim milk and then incubated overnight at 4 °C with a primary antibody, as indicated. The membrane was washed and then incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody. Antibodies against c-Fos, NFATc1, and actin were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Dallas, TX, USA). The protein bands were visualized by using MicroChemi 4.2 (DNR Bio-imaging System, Jerusalem, IL, USA) and Super-Signal West Pico Chemiluminescent Substrate (Pierce Chemical, Rockford, IL, USA).

2.6. Real-Time PCR

Real-time PCR was performed as described previously []. Primers for real-time PCR were designed () by using the Primer3 design program []. Quantitative PCR was completed by using a real-time PCR detection system (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) and TOPreal qPCR 2× PreMIX (Enzynomics, Daejeon, Korea). All tests were run in triplicate, and data were analyzed by the 2method.

2.7. Ovariectomized-Induced Bone Erosion

Eighteen mice of five-week-old female ICR strain (Damool Science, Daejeon, Korea) were randomly divided into 3 groups of 6 mice and ovariectomized (OVX;= 12) or sham-operated (= 6) by the dorsal approach under general anesthesia. The OVX + GE group was administered GE (100 mg/kg of body weight) orally (= 6), while the other groups were administered distilled water (DW; vehicle) orally for 6 weeks daily beginning one day after surgery. At the end of the 6-week treatment period, body and uterus weight of animals were determined by using an electronic scale. Blood samples were maintained at room temperature for 1 h, and centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 5 min to obtain serum. Serum was separated immediately and stored at −80 °C. Serum calcium levels were measured by using a diagnostic slide kit and an automatic analyzer (Fuji Dri-Chem, Fujifilm, Tokyo, Japan). TRAP-activity (a marker of osteoclasts number and activity) was measured by using a TRAP enzyme-linked immunoassay (ELISA) kit (USCN Life Science, Houston, TX, USA). Femurs were obtained from mice sacrificed by cervical dislocation and were fixed in 3.5% formaldehyde for one day. Fixed femurs were scanned and analyzed with a Quantum GX microCT imaging system (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA).

2.8. Statistical Analysis

All quantitative data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) of three replicate experiments. Statistical differences were analyzed by applying a Student’s-test. Probability () values less than 0.05 were considered significant (-values * <0.05, ** <0.01, and *** <0.001).

3. Results

3.1. Extract ofInhibits Osteoclast Differentiation from Macrophages

To determine the potential role of GE in osteoclast differentiation, we evaluated the effects of GE on the ability of RANKL to differentiate BMMs. Cells were incubated with a vehicle (0.1% DW) or GE (at indicated concentrations) in the presence of RANKL (10 ng/mL) and M-CSF (30 ng/mL) for 4 days. The formation of TRAP-multinucleated cells (≥ 3) was induced by RANKL, but GE inhibited such a formation (A). GE reduced the number of TRAP-MNCs in a dose-dependent manner, which effect was observed at GE concentrations greater than 3 μg/mL (B).

3.2. No Cytotoxic Effect of Extract ofon Macrophages

If GE exerts cytotoxicity on the BMMs during culture, osteoclast formation could be inhibited regardless of the effect of GE on osteoclastogenesis. To eliminate this possibility, we performed cell proliferation assays. BMMs were cultured with vehicle (0.1% DW) or GE in the presence of M-CSF (30 ng/mL) for 3 days. As shown inC, GE had no cytotoxic effect on BMMs at the concentrations used in this study.

3.3. Extract ofSuppresses RANKL-Induced c-Fos and NFATc1 Expression

We analyzed the protein expression levels of c-Fos and NFATc1, important regulators of osteoclastogenesis, by Western blotting. RANKL strongly induced protein expression of c-Fos and NFATc1 in osteoclast differentiation, but the c-Fos and NFATc1 protein levels were significantly decreased by GE treatment (A). We further confirmed activity of signaling molecules including JNK, p38, ERK, and I-kB, which are known to play a role in the early stage of RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis, but GE did not decrease the activation of all of them (). Additionally, we observed gene expression of osteoclast-specific markers by undertaking real-time PCR analysis. GE inhibited the mRNA expression of c-Fos and NFATc1 in BMMs treated with RANKL and the mRNA expressions of NFATc1-related genes such as DC-STAMP, cathepsin K, and TRAP in osteoclast differentiation were significantly decreased by GE (B).

3.4. Effects of Extract ofon Serum Biochemical Markers in Ovariectomized Mice

We examined the in vivo effect of GE on bone loss in OVX mice. GE was orally administered daily to OVX mice for six weeks. After six weeks of treatment, we measured body and uterus weights, and assessed serum biochemical marker levels in each mouse. Body weight of the OVX group was significantly greater than the body weight of the sham-operated group, whereas the uterus weight of the OVX group was significantly lower than that of the sham-operated group (A,B). In addition, we determined biochemical marker (calcium and TRAP) levels in serum. The serum calcium and TRAP levels were higher in the OVX group than in the sham-operated group (C,D).

3.5. Extract ofInhibits Bone Loss in Ovariectomized Mice

To examine the effects of GE on bone erosion in OVX mice, femurs obtained from mice were analyzed by a micro-computed tomography (CT) system. In trabecular bone in the femur metaphyseal region, bone mass was decreased in OVX mice, and the administration of GE significantly inhibited the trabecular bone loss (A). Specifically, ovariectomy-mediated changes in bone mineral density (BMD), bone volume/tissue volume (BV/TV), and trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) were significantly prevented by GE.

4. Discussion

Osteoporosis is a major bone disease characterized by low BMD and weakened bone structure. Quality of bone is strongly influenced by the balance of bone-resorbing osteoclast and bone-forming osteoblast activities. Osteoclasts are the only cells that absorb bone and are differentiated from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow []. Moreover, they are formed by the fusion of the mononuclear macrophage lineage []. RANKL and M-CSF are most affected by osteoclast formation [].

In this study, we investigated the effect of GE on RANKL-mediated osteoclast differentiation. BMMs were cultured with RANKL and M-CSF in the presence of GE. The GE completely inhibited TRAP-osteoclasts and exhibited no cytotoxicity at concentrations over 30 μg/mL, and this concentration was used in the following experiment. According to this results, GE has a negative effect on osteoclastogenesis with no cytotoxicity to BMMs.

The TNF-family molecule RANKL is a key regulator of osteoclastogenesis. The binding of RANKL to RANK activates signaling molecules such as MAP kinases (MAPKs), c-Fos, and phospholipase Cγ (PLCγ) that ultimately induce the activation of NFATc1 [,]. Therefore, in order to understand the molecular mechanism of GE inhibition of osteoclast differentiation, the effect of GE on the protein expression level of c-Fos and NFATc1 was analyzed by Western blotting. Protein expression of c-Fos and NFATc1 was strongly inhibited by GE. However, MAPKs, upper signals of c-Fos, were not affected by GE and did not reduce the degradation of I-kB, which indirectly confirmed the activity of NF-kB []. In addition, NFATc1 is an essential transcription factor that regulates osteoclast-specific marker genes such as DC-STAMP, essential for cell-cell fusion, cathepsin K, matrix-degrading enzymes, and TRAP exhibiting bone resorptive activity [,]. In this study, we found that GE inhibits RANKL-induced osteoclast differentiation through the downregulation of c-Fos-NFATc1 signaling.

Furthermore, we identified effects of GE in vivo in an OVX mouse model that has been reported to be useful in skeletal studies []. GE was orally administered to OVX mice for six weeks. The success of OVX surgery was confirmed by observing significant increases in body weight and marked decreases in uterus weight []. In addition, we checked for changes in biochemical markers in serum. Oral administration of GE completely suppressed changes in calcium and TRAP levels. These results indicate that GE inhibits osteoclast differentiation and activation. In addition, we examined the femurs of mice via micro-CT. As shown inA, micro-CT revealed that GE treatment had inhibited OVX-induced bone loss. Histomorphometric analysis of femurs confirmed the inhibitory effects of GE on OVX-induced bone loss in vivo (B) with GE significantly attenuating the OVX-induced changes in BMD, BV/TV, and Tb.Th, but it was not fully recovered. We anticipate that, if we increase the amount of extract in treatment, the difference in results between the sham group and the GE-treated group will decrease.

In summary, GE inhibits osteoclast differentiation by reducing the expression of NFATc1 through the inhibition of c-Fos expression. Moreover, GE can significantly reduce OVX-induced bone loss in vivo. Therefore, GE could be useful when developing a new osteoporosis drug.
articles.abstract: Bone remodeling, a physiological process characterized by bone formation by osteoblasts and bone resorption by osteoclasts, is important for the maintenance of healthy bone in adult humans. Osteoclasts play a critical role in bone erosion and osteoporosis and are bone-specific multinucleated cells generated through differentiation of monocyte/macrophage lineage precursors. Receptor activator of NF-κB ligand (RANKL) has been reported to induce osteoclast differentiation. In this study, we explored whetherextracts (GE) could affect RANKL-mediated osteoclast differentiation. GE significantly inhibited RANKL-activated osteoclast differentiation by inhibiting protein expression of c-fos and nuclear factor of activated T-cells, cytoplasmic 1 (NFATc1), vital factors in RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis. In addition, GE attenuated ovariectomy-induced bone loss in mice. In summary, GE can prevent osteoclastogenesis and hormone-related bone loss via blockage of c-fos-NFATc1 signaling. Our results suggest that GE may have therapeutic potential in the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis.

Introduction

The most promising commodity in the aquaculture sector with the greatest growth potential is the Pacific white shrimp () which is indigenous to the Pacific Ocean []. Because of the exponential growth of this species’ aquaculture, mangrove ecosystems around Asia are being heavily exploited []. This shrimp is known for its quick development, high intensification, low protein requirements, strong tolerance to a broad range of water salinities, and other characteristics that fit highly intensive aquaculture []. However, issues with declining pond habitats have affected shrimp aquaculture, which has led to an increase in stress-induced disease occurrences, primarily with bacterial and viral etiologies [].

In shrimp culture, viral infections are crucial since some of them cause significant crop and financial losses []. White spot disease (WSD) caused by the white spot syndrome virus (WSSV), is a condition that frequently attacks Pacific white shrimp []. WSSV, an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus, is recognized as agenus in thefamily []. Since its initial appearance in Taiwan in the 1990s, the WSSV has quickly expanded to places used for shrimp aquaculture worldwide []. Because of its extreme virulence, which can cause 100% shrimp mortality within a few days of infection and result in significant financial deprivation for the business, WSSV is still one of the most critical diseases affecting shrimp mariculture [,]. When shrimp are infected with WSSV, they become very weak, lose interest in food, and typically get it to the embankment’s edge before passing away []. Other features of WSSV include sluggishness, detached cuticle, frequently reddish discoloration, and white patches on the carapace, appendages, and the cuticle, measuring between 0.5 and 2.0 mm in diameter [,]. The addition of an immunostimulant derived from ecologically acceptable plant materials is an attempt to stop the WSSV attack in penaeid shrimp production with no health hazards to the consumer or the environment [,]. Since it initially appeared in the early 1990s and spread to all of the main shrimp-producing nations, WSD has grown to be the biggest danger to shrimp production. WSD is predicted to continue causing about US$1 billion in economic losses each year, with estimates of the disease’s overall economic harm ranging from US$8 to US$15 billion [].

Shrimp, like other invertebrates, lack adaptive immunity and have only developed an innate immune system in which circulating hemocytes, such as granular cells (GCs), hyaline cells (HCs), and semi-granular cells (SGCs), are essential for protecting against pathogenic microorganisms []. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), which are foreign polysaccharides, are recognized and bound by host proteins known as pattern recognition proteins (PRPs) to initiate innate immunity. This leads to cellular and hematological reactions such as phagocytosis, nodulation, coagulation, and the prophenoloxidase (proPO) cascade, as well as the induction of antimicrobial peptide synthesis []. The phenoloxidase enzyme (PO) is activated by the proPO system after infection and/or dietary immunostimulant integration. This initiates the melanization process, which inactivates the foreign particles and shields the host from pathogen damage [,]. Circulating hemocytes also remove foreign particles by phagocytosis []. After a foreign particle binds to a cell, the membrane-bound enzyme complex NADPH oxidase assembles to start the process. It reduces molecular oxygen to form superoxide anions, which react to produce other reactive oxygen species (ROS) like hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radical, and singlet oxygen []. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) scavenges superoxide anions to produce hydrogen peroxide, which glutathione peroxidase (GPx) or catalase subsequently reduces. The first byproduct of this process, referred to as respiratory bursts (RBs), is superoxide anions []. Moreover, the three primary signaling mechanisms that control shrimp innate immunity are the toll pathway, the immunological deficiency (IMD) pathway, and the Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) pathway []. In order to carry out the immune responses against pathogen invasion, the signaling pathway’s activation leads to the production of several immune-related genes, including lysozyme, prophenoloxidase (proPO), and anti-microbial peptides (AMPs) []. In shrimp humoral immune responses, anti-microbial peptides such as crustins, penaeidins, and anti-lipopolysaccharide factor (ALF) are thought to be the most significant effector molecules with effective antimicrobial activity []. Another carbohydrate recognition protein is C-type lectin (CTL) which is mainly responsible for pathogen recognition as it can recognize and bind to a specific cell surface, viral carbohydrates, and glycoproteins for induction antiviral peptides [].

Shrimp have thus far been exposed to a variety of immunostimulants, including marine yeast [,], macroalgae [,], , seaweed [,], and microalgae [,]. Regarding immunostimulants, seaweeds are a rich source of bioactive substances that are highly valued by the food and pharmaceutical industries, including polysaccharides and pigments [,]. The use of dry, isolated components and/or extracts of seaweeds (red, brown, and green) as an aquafeed ingredient in shrimp farming is becoming more widely recognized []. Various characteristics include immune-modulatory, nutritional, growth-promoting, antibacterial, cytostatic, neuroprotective, antifungal, antioxidant, antiviral and hepatoprotective activities [–].

A common red seaweed,, is a naturally occurring plant material that has the potential to be assessed as a secure and eco-friendly immunostimulant [].has been extensively farmed as a common source of agar []. According to the chemical investigation,is primarily composed of polysaccharides, as evidenced by the seaweed’s sugars (95.40%) and sulfate (3.4%) contents [,]. According to Jasmanindara et al. [] and Rudi et al. [], potent-sulfated polysaccharides that were derived fromcan functionally be used as immune stimulators for shrimp and boost immunity against infection. In tiger shrimp resistant to WSSV, the sulfate inbinds to galactose as galactan sulfate, which is a potential immune stimulant substance [,]. Previous reports by Arulkumar et al. [] and Mubarak et al. [] demonstrated thatextract includes such as phenolic compounds, tannins, quinones, terpenoids, saponins, and flavonoids that could shield the cells and fight against a variety of diseases. Due to the presence of large amounts of polyphenols and sulfated polysaccharides, this seaweed has been shown to lessen the invasion of free radicals in tissues by reducing oxidative distress []. In addition to being an immunological stimulant,may accelerate the shrimp’s pace of growth. White shrimp grew more quickly when fed a diet containing 2 g/kgextract following previous studies by Jasminandar et al. [] and Ihsan et al. [].

Thus, this study explored the influence of short-term supplementingonimmunological parameters including the hemocyte count, ACP, AKP, PO and lysozyme activities as well as phagocytosis, ROS, antioxidant activity (SOD, CAT, and GPx), and immune-related genes (ALF1, CRU1, PEN4, CTL, TRAF6, STAT, TLR1, and NOS). The resistance offed oncontaining diets against WSSV infection was also evaluated.

Materials and methods

Virus propagation

The WSSV was originally isolated from infected cultured shrimp in Vietnam. Following the steps outlined by Motamedi Sedeh et al. [], infected juvenilewere used to isolate WSSV (IRWSSVBU1), which was then homogenized in TNE buffer (0.05 M Tris, 0.1 M NaCl, 0.001 M EDTA, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 4000 g for 15 min at 4 °C. Filtration of the supernatant was done using a millipore (0.45 mm). To propagate the WSSV, 100 healthycrayfish were injected intramuscularly with 100 ml of the prepared supernatant. A portion of the crayfish appendage tissues was cut, collected, and homogenized to be tested using the Nested-PCR (IQ 2000 diagnostic kit, GeneReach Biotechnology Corp., Taiwan). Hemolymph was removed from infected shrimp and virus stocks were isolated using sucrose gradient centrifugation following the previously explained protocol []. The virus’ copy number was identified using qRT-PCR. Aliquots of virus samples were kept at − 80 °C.

Three or four shrimp were infected with WSSV stock suspension (–80 °C) to reactivate the virus before the challenge. One gram of the contaminated shrimp organ was taken, pounded into a fine powder, and then added to nine milliliters of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution. The solution was then centrifuged twice, for a total of thirty minutes at a speed of 3000 rpm and twenty minutes at a speed of 8000 rpm. Using a syringe and a filter holder with 0.45 μm filtering paper, the obtained supernatant was filtered. To infect Pacific white shrimp with WSSV, an injection was used. The third segment of the abdomen was injected intramuscularly with 0.1 ml of viral solution (1.4 × 10copies/ml). The PBS alone was injected into the negative control shrimp [].

Experimental design, sampling, and challenge test

Three hundred and sixty healthy shrimp with average body weight (15.26 g ± 1.29 g) were obtained from the El-Ekhlas shrimp hatchery in Damietta- Port Said Province, Egypt. The shrimp were housed in an indoor setup system running with natural seawater. Water quality parameters can be measured with the LaMotteAquaponics Test Kit (LaMotte Company, Chestertown, MD, USA), including salinity (‰) using a salinometer along with the pH value, dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L) using an oximeter model YK-22DO, temperature (C) using a water thermometer (Yellow Springs Comp., Yellow Springs, OH, USA), and many others were measured every day. Throughout the experimental period, shrimp water quality was maintained [salinity (30‰), DO (5.00-6.30 mg L), pH (7.6 ± 0.3), and temperature (25 ± 2C) were made. The shrimp were fed their respective diets (4% of their body weight) at 08:00 and 19:00 h. Following the welfare and ethical approval of laboratory animals, the shrimp was allowed to have adequate nutrition and proper water quality. The shrimp was also allowed to exhibit normal behavior patterns. The shrimp also was protected from pain, suffering, injury, and disease.

A composite sand filter was employed in the experiment to filter the seawater. Following their acclimation period, the shrimp were randomly divided into 120-liter fiber tanks (30 shrimp/tank). Each diet plan was assigned a triple tank (a total of 90 shrimp/ group). Both control and dried seaweed-containing diets, namely 0, 2, 4, and 8 g kgdiet [,], were given to the shrimp. After 21 days of the feeding period, 10 shrimp were collected from each tank. Hemolymph (100 µl) was collected from each shrimp into a syringe containing 900 µl of anticoagulant solution (Trisodium citrate 30 mM, sodium chloride 0.34 M, EDTA 10 mM, pH 7.5, osmolality 780 mOsm kg/1). Hemocytometers were used to measure cell density and trypan blue exclusion tests were used to assess cell viability. To estimate ROS generation, and phagocytic activity, harvested cells were adjusted to 5 × 10cells/ml. The gills were minced and mixed with a shrimp PBS (pH 7.4) in a homogenizer yielding a homogenate that was then centrifuged forming a supernatant to be used in the estimation of ACP, AKP, SOD, GPx, catalase, and MDA. To be employed in the RNA extraction, gills (= 5) were also obtained from shrimp in each group while maintaining sterility.

Following the use of RT-PCR to determine the virus’ copy number, the WSSV filtrate was used for the challenge test. The remaining shrimp from each group (60 shrimp/ group) received an intramuscular injection of 0.1 ml of WSSV (1.4 × 10copies/ml). After injection, all shrimp groups were maintained in the same experimental tanks with the same conditions. WSSV infection-related symptoms were verified by looking for the distinctive white patches on the dead shrimp carapace. The polymerase chain reaction (RCR) test for DNA samples was randomly taken from the dead samples’ gills in each group and made also to confirm infection. Following the challenge with WSSV, the shrimp were fed diets with and without dried seaweed supplements. The shrimp were examined to check for signs of illness. The shrimp mortality in each tank was tracked for ten days, and the survival percentage was calculated by averaging the tanks in triplicate. The same samples as before the challenge were collected on the 5th day of the challenge.

Reaction conditions for the WSSV gene amplification

According to Saberi et al. [] the oligonucleotide primers for WSSV F 5’ GTGACCAAGACCATCGAAAC 3’ and R 5’ TCAGTCATCTTGAAGTAGCC 3’ were as follows. That was intended to amplify (234 bp) all of the vp28 ORFs in the WSSV PCR: Using the GeneAmp Polymerase Chain Reaction (Creacon, Thermo cycler, Holand) system cycler, specific DNA was amplified. To obtain amplified genomic DNA, PCR was used. The cycling parameters for the second step reaction were as follows: a single cycle at 95 °C for two minutes, followed by 39 cycles at 95 °C, 65 °C, and 72 °C for 30 s each, and a final extension for two minutes at 72 °C [].

Total hemocyte count

Using a hemocytometer (Boeco, Hamburg, Germany) and a 400x magnification light microscope, the total hemocyte count (THC) was determined.

A mixture of anticoagulant and hemolymph was treated for 20 min at room temperature with fixative (10% formalin in 0.45 M NaCl). After adding the same volume of rose bengal solution (1.2% rose bengal in 50% ethanol) to fixed hemocyte suspensions (20 µL), the mixture was incubated for an additional 20 min at 25 °C. After the smears were ready, they were fully air-dried and then counterstained for ten minutes using a hematoxylin solution. After counting at least 200 cells on each slide, the counts, and relative proportions of different hemocyte types were determined [(number of distinct hemocyte cell types / 200) x THC] [].

Phagocytic activity

With a small modification, phagocytic activity was measured using Xian et al. [] methodology. After gently mixing 500 µl of cell suspensions (5 × 10cells/mL), the same volume of latex beads (~ 10beads/mL; 1.094µ; Polysciences, USA) was added, and the mixture was incubated for 30 min at room temperature. The hemocyte bead mixture was fixed for 20 min at room temperature using the same volume of 10% formalin. Rose bengal and hematoxylin solutions were used to stain the hemocytes in the manner previously mentioned []. Phagocytosis (%) equals (phagocytic hemocytes / total hemocytes) x 100.

ROS production

Using a fluorescent probe called 2’,7’-dichlorofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA), intracellular ROS was measured using a modified technique as reported by Moss and Allam []. When reactive oxygen species (ROS) are present, DCFH-DA diffuses across the cell membrane and is enzymatically hydrolyzed by intracellular esterases to generate non-fluorescent 2’,7’-dichlorofluorescein (DCFH). This is subsequently quickly oxidized to form highly fluorescent 2’,7’-dichlorofluorescin (DCF). It is thought that the intensity of DCF fluorescence correlates with the quantity of ROS produced inside cells. At first, DCFH was thought to be a particular HOindication. Later on, though, it was shown that nitric oxide (NO), peroxynitrite, hydroxyl (HO), and peroxyl (ROO) could also oxidize it (Xian et al., 2009). A final concentration of 0.1 mM of 2′, 7′-dichlorofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA, Sigma) was incubated for 30 min at room temperature with 100 µl of hemolymph (5 × 105 cells/mL). Zymosan suspensions were added at a ratio of 1 hemocyte: 50 particles to directly trigger the formation of ROS. Using Varioskan Flash Spectral Scanning Multimode Readers (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), the fluorescence reading was obtained at 502 nm excitation and 523 nm emission wavelengths following a 30-minute dark incubation period.

Lysozyme activity

The ability of the lysozyme to lyse(Sigma Chemical Co., USA) was used to determine its activity, as per the previously published technique []. Briefly, the precipitate obtained from centrifuging the hemolymph-anticoagulant mixture was combined with 0.02%diluted in shrimp saline. Using a microplate reader (Optica, Mikura Ltd, UK), the absorbance was measured at 1-minute intervals for 5 min at 540 nm after the reaction was administered at room temperature. Using lyophilized chicken egg-white lysozyme (Sigma, USA), a calibration curve was used to determine the lysozyme concentration.

Phenoloxidase activity

The production of dopachrome from L-dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-DOPA; Sigma, USA) was used to evaluate phenoloxidase (PO) activity, as previously reported by Hernández-López et al. []. Following homogenization of the suspensions (Hemolymph and cacodylate (CAC) buffer) using Pellet Pestles (Sigma-Aldrich, USA), the mixtures were centrifuged for 20 min at 15,000 rpm. Hemocyte lysate supernatant (HLS), the end product, was extracted and utilized as an enzyme source right away. Incubated at 25 °C, 200 µl of HLS were added to the same volume of trypsin (1 mg/mL CAC buffer). Following a 30-minute incubation period, 200 µl of L-DOPA (3 mg/mL CAC buffer) was introduced. Using Varioskan Flash Spectral Scanning Multimode Readers (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), the optical density was measured at 490 nm. According to Sung et al. [], the phenoloxidase activity was determined as an increase in the optical density of 0.001/min/ mg protein. The Bradford [] technique was used to determine the protein content of HLS.

Alkaline and acid phosphatase activities

Assays for alkaline (ALP) and acid phosphatase (ACP) activities were carried out using the guidelines provided by Vaseeharan et al. []. In summary, p-nitro phenyl phosphate (16 mM) was used as a standard substrate for the measurement of ALP and ACP. The ALP and ACP tests were conducted using glycine NaOH buffer and sodium acetate buffer, respectively. The hemolymph (50 µL) and the substrate (200 µL) were added to mixtures, which were then incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. At 410 nm, the amount of released p-nitrophenol in the resultant supernatants was measured and determined using the standard curve.

Oxidant/antioxidant status

Superoxide dismutase (SOD, Catalog NO.; EIASODC), Catalase (CAT, Catalog NO.; EIACATC), glutathione peroxidase (GPx, Catalog NO.; EEA010) and malondialdehyde (MDA, Catalog NO.; EEA015) were measured using colorimetric detection kits (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Karlsruhe, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s protocols.

The enzyme’s capacity to stop the phenazine methosulfate-mediated reduction of nitroblue tetrazolium dye at a wavelength of 560 nm was used to evaluate SOD []. The CAT was computed using the enzyme reaction mixture, which included contained samples, hydrogen peroxide (HO), and potassium phosphate (pH 7.0). A UV–VIS spectrophotometer set at 240 nm was used to calculate the molar attenuation coefficient of HO[]. GPx activity was measured in tissue homogenate. In summary, 200 µL of homogenate supernatant was combined with 1 mL of pH 7.0 phosphate buffer, 10 mL glutathione (150 mM), 10 mL glutathione reductase (340 U/mL), 30 mL (25 mM EDTA), 30 mL NADPH (5 mM), 10 mL Triton X-100 (20%), and 50 µL H 33 2 NADP + O 2 (7.5mM). For three minutes, the oxidation of NADPH was monitored at 340 nm []. The thiobarbituric acid technique was used to determine the MDA level. Thiobarbituric acid’s reactive components were measured at 535 nm and then expressed in terms of MDA produced [].

RNAiso Plus (TAKARA, Japan) was used to extract total RNA from various tissue samples in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Discussion

During recent decades, scientific research has focused on the impact of seaweeds as feed additives on the amelioration of the survival rates, healthy condition, immune response, and disease resistance of cultured fish and shrimp species [,]. In the present study, we evaluated the positive effect of dietary seaweedsupplementation on the white spot syndrome resistance of the shrimp was positive as the results of the viral challenge test showed that the seaweed-supplemented diet can protect against viral WSSV infection. Indeed, the-based dietary supplement markedly improved shrimp survival rates against the WSSV. This result conferred the interesting fact given the prospective antiviral protection by dietary inclusion ofin shrimp. A diet supplemented with extract fromat 4 g kgdose was shown to be also useful in the protection against WSSV infection in Pacific white shrimp []. In addition, shrimp white shrimpreceiving extracts ofat 2.0 g kgrevealed potential protection with higher survival rates against() infection [], as well as, againstor/ and WSSV pathogens []. The survival rate was significantly increased in whiteleg shrimp supplemented withextracted diet and exposed to WSSV injection []. Effectively, bioactive compounds contained inspecies, such as polyunsaturated fatty acids (omega-3 fatty acids (ɷ-3)), sulfated polysaccharides (e.g., agar and carrageenan, sulphated galactans, and porphyrans), and lectins, have been largely associated with antiviral defenses via competing with WSSV entry to target tissues [,,], giving their ability to boost the innate immunity of shrimp post-WSSV challenge as evidenced by gradual vanishing of white spots in supplemented shrimp exposed to WSSV. It was previously reported that shrimp could resist a wide range of infectious pathogen attacks because immunostimulants swiftly initiate phagocytosis and the generation of ROS []. The current study’s findings regarding the stimulation of non-specific immunity through the promotion of hemocyte count, ACP, AKP, PO, and lysozyme activities as well as phagocytosis, ROS, antioxidant activity, and induction of immune genes in shrimp may be partially responsible for the enhanced resistance ofagainst WSSV infection. Additionally, these findings support the theory that seaweed supplements improve host health by inducing immunological responses that protect against pathogenic microorganisms []. Consequently, addingto shrimp diets could be a useful way to lessen the negative effects of WSSV on shrimp aquaculture.

Immune defenses of shrimp are represented by hemocytes which have a crucial role in both cellular and humoral immunity [–]. Besides, hemocyte count is a reliable indicator of penaeid shrimp health status []. In the present study, whiteleg shrimp juveniles fedat 4.0 and 8.0 g kgdiets before and after viral challenge, exhibited increased THCs, HCs, GCs, and SGCs. Incorporation ofextract containing diets at 2.0 g kgfor 14 days showed marked augmentation in THCs together with HCs, GCs, and SGCs []. As well, the dietary administration ofextract at 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, and 5.0 g kghas increased the total hemocyte counts in normal supplemented and challenged Pacific white shrimp with white spot syndrome virus []. Total hemocyte counts have been significantly increased in the infected whiteleg shrimp withand supplemented with 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 g kgdoses of[,]. Notably, the increment that occurred in the total and differential hemocytes indicated that crude sulfated polysaccharides (SPs) derived fromcan stimulate innate hemocyte receptors in shrimp, hence increasing shrimp body humoral and cellular immune reactive defenses []. A similar increment is exhibited following the WSSV challenge via recognition of WSSV-associated molecular pattern particles (PAMP) by the hemocyte cell receptors [,]. Indeed, the imperative immunostimulatory effect of incorporatedextract in diets of shrimp and prawns has been documented, subsequent to increasing the immune system and their survival against microbial pathogens attack [,].

Phagocytosis is an indispensable mechanism of shrimp innate cellular immunity, which is initiated by recognizing the target particles via hyaline cells for phagosome formation, endocytosis, and engulfing of microbial pathogens [,]. Following this mechanism, the oxygen-dependent respiratory burst produces superoxide anion and oxygen reactive species (ROS) formation to remove the invading pathogens within phagosome bodies [,]. Whereas, humoral immunity involves the hemocyte’s secretion of prophenoloxidase system (proPO), lysozyme, and other antimicrobial peptides (crustins and lectins), which can trigger various immune responses []. During infection and/or dietary immunostimulant incorporation, the proPO system activates the phenoloxidase enzyme (PO), which triggers the melanization process to inactivate the foreign particles, and to protect the host against pathogens damage [,]. Antimicrobial lysozyme is a substantial component of nonspecific immunity in penaeid shrimp that can defend against pathogenic microbes by catalyzing the hydrolysis of the bacterial cell walls [,]. The current study displayed thatpowder in feed significantly increased the phagocytosis, PO, ROS, and lysozyme activities of hemocytes in, pre-and post-WSSV challenge. Additional studies have shown thatshrimp fedpowder (5.0 g kg), increased the activity of phagocytosis, respiratory bursts, lysozyme, and PO []. Similarly, dietaryextract markedly increased the PO and phagocytic activities, and respiratory burst ofbefore and after[,,], as well as WSSV infection []. The higher plasma peroxidase and lysozyme activities were manifested in rainbow trout () fed with 5%[]. It is reported that the immunostimulantextract has a significant effect on enhancing the immune system ofchallenged with WSSV via increasing phagocytosis and respiratory burst []. Interestingly, these results were consistent with the THCs and differential hemocyte counts in our study, showing that hemocyte numbers of shrimp are positively correlated with phagocytic activity and ROS intermediates viasupplementation, which could improve the number of hyaline cells involved in the phagocytotic activity of crustaceans [,]. Subsequently, notable hemocyte ROS production in shrimp exhibited in feed supplemented withindicated by higher phagocytic activity and oxygen-dependent killing mechanism of WSSV viral particles. We also speculated that the higher activity of PO and lysozyme is related to the interaction of sulfated galactans contained in red seaweedwith-1, 3-glucan binding protein on the hemocytes membrane to stimulate their receptors to enhance the PO enzyme activation [,]. Thus, phenoloxidase activity can identify the foreign particles that enter the shrimp body to initiate melanin production during infection. To our knowledge, it has been documented that the major polysaccharide (agar) contained in the cell walls ofspp. is responsible for the modulation of the immunological response in fish species [,].

From another perspective, phosphatase enzymes are reliable indicators for lysosomal enzymes that are released by hemocytes, taking part in the growth and nonspecific immune capacity in shrimp []. ALP is involved in the regulation of cellular metabolic functions, such as growth and nutrient transport as well as and it stores microbes in lysosomes []. ACP digests the invading organisms in aquatic crustaceans []. In our present study, there were significantly higher gills ACP and ALK activities in groups feddiets pre- and post-WSSV challenge. Similarly, an elevated trend in AKP and ACP activities was manifested infed sulfate-based alginate polysaccharide extracted from red seaweeds []. Higher ACP activity was displayed in white leg shrimp supplemented with seaweedextract []. During cold stress, the incorporation of brown seaweed,into shrimp diets markedly increased the levels of ACP and ALK []. We suggest that polysaccharides (agar) inmay be responsible for the improved immune enzyme activity ofduring viral infection.

Antioxidant enzymes play remarkable roles in the shrimp’s immune defense by scavenging the superoxide anions and other ROS produced by hemocytes to minimize the oxidative stress as excess ROS production can oxidize the fatty acids that compose cell membranes, generating lipid peroxides like malondialdehyde (MDA) [,]. Our study revealed that white shrimp juveniles fed-containing diets after 21 days exhibited increased SOD, CAT, and GPx activity, altogether with decreased MDA levels post supplementation and challenge test. SOD enzymes stimulate the conversion of superoxide (O) free radicles into hydrogen peroxide (HO) and oxygen to avoid host tissue damage from excess free radicals []. While GPx and CAT enzymes decompose the abundant HOgenerated by phagocytes during the immune reactions into water (HO) and O[]. In addition, reduction of the lipid hydroperoxides can be conducted via GPx []. The dietary administration ofextract at 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 g kgfor 16 weeks increased SOD activity in the hemolymph of white shrimp []. The muscle SOD activity was also increased in white leg shrimp supplemented with 5%pre- and post-white spot syndrome virus infection []. White shrimp,fedextract at 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 g kgfor 14 days showed an increase in SOD and GPx activities in the hemolymph []. It has been reported that juvenile white shrimp fed with, significantly increased the enzyme activities of SOD, GPx, and CAT and diminished the content of MDA in the hepatopancrease of shrimps []. Nevertheless, increased the activity of hepatic catalase and glutathione reductase enzymes was assessed in the gilthead seabream () fedbefore and after challenge withsubsp.[]. Thus, the increment in the antioxidant targets along with reduced MDA content insupplemented groups prohibit the burst of cellular free radicles during defense against WSSV infections and safeguard shrimp cells from damage that is supported by the effective protective impact ofsupplementation in the normal cellular functions and scavenging ROS intermediates in normal and infectedshrimp.sp. seaweeds can be utilized as a source of natural antioxidant compounds because of their active polyphenolic compounds (e.g., phenolic acids, flavonoids, phlorotannins, fucoxanthin, and bromophenols), terpenoids (- and-carotene, lutein, and zeaxanthin), and alkaloids [], which they play essential functions in decreasing the lipid peroxidation along with enhancing the antioxidant capability against oxidative stress [,]. Besides, dietary red seaweedsupplementation has been assessed as a vector for vitamins and halogenated minerals, which have antioxidation characteristics [].

Shrimp humoral immunity involves the release of antimicrobial peptides from granular and semi-granular hemocytes, which can trigger various immune responses through intercellular communication. C-type lectins (CTLs) are Cadependent carbohydrate recognition proteins that are mainly responsible for pathogen recognition, and cell-cell interactions as they can recognize and bind to a specific cell surface and viral carbohydrates (saccharides) and glycoproteins for pathogens and hemocytes agglutination []. As well, CTLs are involved in the phagocytic activity, activation of proPO, melanization, and antiviral activationbinding to the envelope proteins of WSSV []. Crustins (CRU1), penaeidins (PEN4), and antilipolysaccharide factors (ALF1) are major antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) that restrain the bacterial growth inside the hemolymph of crustaceans []. Crustins are cationic proteins against Gram-positive bacteria; penaeidins are proline/arginine-rich peptides, that possess antimicrobial activities against both Gram-positive and -negative bacteria, as well as a potent chitin-binding activity of fungi []. ALFs are large proteins, exhibiting strong bactericidal activity and interfering with WSSV viral particle replication []. The results of the current research showed that dietaryin three different doses effectively stimulated the expression of ALF1, CRU1, PEN4, and CTL genes in the gills of unchallenged shrimp. On the 7th day of WSSV infection, the expression of studied genes in all groups was notably downregulated. However, after the challenge with the WSSV, the expression levels of these genes in these previous groups were upregulated bysupplementation in a dose-dependent manner. The gene expressions of lectin and penaeidin 3 were up-regulated in the hemocytes of shrimp that received carrageenan, a red seaweed polysaccharide at 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 g kgfor 3 weeks []. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) is a crucial pattern recognition receptor (PRR), which senses and binds to specific pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) of microbes to trigger signaling pathways (e.g., TLR-TRAF6, IMD, and JAK-STAT) involved in immune responses of shrimp [,]. Tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) is a pivotal signal transducer of TLR proteins mediated signaling pathway (TLR-TRAF6) [], which is activated by PAMPs to activate nuclear factor-kappa B and transcript many pro-inflammatory genes as well as it activates the AMPs to combat viral infections [,]. TRAF6 expression was markedly induced by WSSV andchallenge in various shrimp species [,]. The same trend was observed in the expression of TLRs in shrimp after WSSV infection []. The signal transducer and activator of the transcription (STAT) gene has an important part of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway as it phosphorylated and dimerized during shrimp antiviral immunity against WSSV [], as well as shrimp STAT is known to bind to the promoter region of the WSSV immediate early promotor gene ie1 to enhance its expression, subsequently, the expression of STAT was increased after WSSV infection []. Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) catalyzes the formation of the free radical Nitric oxide (NO), which is produced by hemocytes during phagocytosis during viral infection by directly damaging the DNA, protein, and lipid of pathogen membrane []. In the present study, the transcript levels of TRAF6, STAT, TLR1, and NOS in the gills of challenged control white shrimp were increased, however, they significantly downregulated insupplemented challenged shrimp, except for NOS. Taken together, these data indicate that these genes participate in the regulation of innate immune responses of shrimp against WSSV infections by increasing their expression. At the same time, considering the WSSV host interaction, it could be proposed that sulfated galactan contained inbinding with TLRs interrupted the viral utilization of the TLR-TRAF and JAK-STAT signaling pathways for viral replication in the host cell for preserving immune homeostasis.

However, THCs and differential hemocytes, as well as most of the immune parameters in control shrimps markedly declined within ten days of WSSV infection. Then, it was notably recovered and enhanced at various doses ofon day 10 of infection. The notable decrease in circulating hemocytes in viral-infected shrimp has been reported in many studies from hemocytes leaving the circulation and migrating to tissues; or it could be due to the restricted hematopoiesis to the hematopoietic tissue from WSSV invasion [,]. Consequently, most cellular, and humoral immunity reactions may also be diminished as observed in control shrimp challenged with WSSV.

Because brown seaweeds contain polysaccharides including laminarin, alginate, and fucoidan., they can be utilized as an immunostimulant []. Through interactions with dectin-1 receptors on the surface of immune cells, seaweed polysaccharides can activate the non-specific immune system including phagocytic and respiratory burst activities []. Seaweed polysaccharides when added to food can help aquatic animals grow, strengthen their immune systems against viruses and bacteria, and improve their gut health and antioxidant capacity []. According to Ale et al. [], fucoidan derived from brown seaweed, contains polysaccharide sulfate, which has immunomodulatory effects. The sulfate present inis coupled to galactose since sulfated galactans are an immunostimulator in tiger prawns and increase resistance to WSSV infection []. Other important pattern recognition proteins (PRPs), lipopolysaccharide and b-1,3-glucan-binding protein (LGBP) recognize lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and b-1,3-glucan (bG), sometimes referred to as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), and thereby initiate innate immunity in[]. In addition to binding to LPS and bG, recombinant LGBP (rLvLGBP) also binds to fucoidan, laminarin, and alginate from seaweed. This resulted in the degranulation of shrimp hemocytes, and activation of the proPO system that subsequently leading to an increase in PO activity, indicating the stimulation of innate immunity [].

Conclusion

According to the current study, shrimp-fed diets containing(GV) extract demonstrated enhanced immunity as evidenced by increases in circulating hemocyte c, ACP, AKP, PO and lysozyme activities as well as phagocytosis, ROS, antioxidant activity (SOD, CAT, and GPx), and immune-related genes (ALF1, CRU1, PEN4, CTL, TRAF6, STAT, TLR1, and NOS). In addition, adding GV to shrimp meal greatly increases their resistance to white spot disease brought on by WSSV infections. The ideal dose of dietary GV treatment for pacific white shrimp is 8 g GV (kg diet), which will increase their immunity and disease resistance.
